card.hook: Here's a surprise: the best photo of the Temple of the Tooth isn't taken at its gates. Guides call the view from above the classic postcard shot, and it's free.
card.stand_here: Head for Kandy View Point, the built platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, to the south-east and uphill from the Temple of the Tooth beside Kandy Lake. It's about 25 minutes on foot. Face north-west and you'll see the temple among the rooftops, with the lake and green hills around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide view of lake, hills and rooftops. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the temple itself, because it looks small in the wide shot. If the platform is crowded and you need to step back, zoom 0.5x helps.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top third line so the lake and rooftops fill the bottom, then tap the temple and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or just before sunset, when the crowds are smaller and the light is softer. At sunset you might also catch the city lights coming on.
card.selfie_here: Try the stone path outside the moat: use the front camera and stand with the white walls and red-tiled spires filling the frame behind you. Hold the phone a little low, or use zoom 0.5x, to fit more of the roofs in.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is restricted inside the temple, so stick to exterior shots and check the signs. Don't pose for selfies with your back to a shrine or Buddha image. Cover your shoulders and knees, and expect a bag search and a security checkpoint on the way in.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the platform, one wide for the setting and one zoomed in on the temple roofs, then see if you can spot the white spires hiding among the rooftops.
card.good_to_know: The Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic (Sri Dalada Maligawa) holds the tooth relic of the Buddha and sits in the old Royal Palace Complex, part of a World Heritage Site. The temple you see today was built under Vira Narendra Sinha, and the octagonal Paththirippuwa and the moat came later, under Sri Vikrama Rajasinha. The Kandy Esala Perahera is held every year to pay homage to the relic.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Kandy View Point, the built platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, to the south-east and uphill from the Temple of the Tooth beside Kandy Lake. It's about 25 minutes on foot. Face north-west and you'll see the temple among the rooftops, with the lake and green hills around it.

selfie_spots.why: Guides describe this exterior as the photo-friendly view of the temple's Kandyan roofs and walls, and it sits outside the restricted interior.

card.hook: Picture two tall rows of royal palms racing away from you until they seem to meet in the distance. This is the postcard view of Peradeniya, and the symmetry does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Royal Palm Avenue, straight ahead from the main entrance, about 300 m along the palm-lined River Drive. Start at the entrance end and face down the length of the avenue so the palms run away from you in two straight rows.
card.zoom: Use 1x for the main shot down the avenue. Try 0.5x if you want the palms to look even taller, but keep the phone level so the rows don't lean. From further back, 2x squeezes the palms closer together, which can look striking.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the middle of the path on the centre line, then tap the far end of the avenue and slide it a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Aim for the first hour after the gardens open. The light along the avenue is at its best then, and the path is likely to be quieter too.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of Royal Palm Avenue, so the palm rows frame you on both sides, and use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) to catch them over your shoulder. For a history-flavoured selfie, stand beside the Zhou Enlai tree, slightly angled, with its wooden plaque in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the bridge or lawn next to the Flower Garden, a short distance back, and shoot toward you while you stand with the palm avenue or flower garden behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The sun is very strong here, so bring sunscreen, a hat and water. The gardens are a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go for entry details and any closures.
card.challenge: Can you get both rows of palms to mirror each other perfectly? Bonus points for one tiny person far down the path to show how tall the trees are.
card.good_to_know: The gardens cover 147 acres beside the Mahaweli River and hold more than 4,000 species of plants, from orchids and spices to many kinds of palm. The garden was formally established in 1843. Elsewhere in the grounds you can find the Cannonball Tree planted by King George V and Queen Mary in 1901.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Royal Palm Avenue, straight ahead from the main entrance, about 300 m along the palm-lined River Drive. Start at the entrance end and face down the length of the avenue so the palms run away from you in two straight rows.

selfie_spots.why: Guides say the plaque plus tree bark give a sense of history, and the garden is visible behind the tree when you stand beside it.

card.hook: Most people expect Kandy Lake to be best when you're standing right beside it. It's actually at its prettiest from up the hill, where it sits calmly in the middle of the picture like a postcard.
card.stand_here: Head for Kandy View Point, the viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, on the hill to the south-west of the lake and roughly 2 km from it. Face north-east, and the lake, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic and the green hills are all in front of you. The walk is steep, so a short tuk-tuk ride is the easy option.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the lake, the temple and the hills in one frame. If you can't squeeze it all in, drop to zoom 0.5x for a wider view. For a closer shot, zoom in on the island and the pale wall along the shore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line, so the lake and rooftops fill most of the frame.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is the favourite, when the city lights start to come on, and sunrise is also recommended. The platform is small and can get busy around sunset, so arrive a little early to claim your spot.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the single stone chair at Kandy View Point, with the lake and city behind you. Use the front camera and hold it a bit higher than usual. Try zoom 0.5x if you want more of the view over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The platform has limited room and roadside parking gets congested at busy times, so allow extra time if you come by car. The lakeside path may close during festivals or ceremonies, so check locally before you go.
card.challenge: Get the lake as the middle layer of your picture, with hills above, town below and the horizon dead level on the gridline. Bonus points if the chair sneaks into the frame.
card.good_to_know: King Sri Wickrama Rajasinghe had the lake made in 1807 next to the Temple of the Tooth, turning old paddy fields into water. The low white scalloped wall along the shore is called the Clouds Wall and runs for roughly 630 metres. Its triangular openings were once used for oil lamps on festival days, and the whole lake is about 3.2 km around.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Kandy View Point, the viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, on the hill to the south-west of the lake and roughly 2 km from it. Face north-east, and the lake, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic and the green hills are all in front of you. The walk is steep, so a short tuk-tuk ride is the easy option.

selfie_spots.name: Kandy View Point (Arthur's Seat), the single chair on the platform
selfie_spots.detail: on the iconic single stone chair at the Kandy View Point platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha, with the lake and city in the background
selfie_spots.why: The chair is the viewpoint's known prop, and it frames you against Kandy Lake and the city below.

Sources note the viewpoint involves a short but steep uphill walk or a tuk-tuk ride, and mention hawkers and a crowded roadside, but no page gave a specific safety point.

card.hook: Here's the surprise: from this terrace, Queen's Hotel isn't the star, it's one landmark in a big, hazy Kandy town portrait. Think postcard of the whole town, with the hotel tucked in like an Easter egg.
card.stand_here: Stand on the terrace at Kandy View Point, on higher ground south-east of the centre. The hotel lies to the north-west, about 1.7 km away in a straight line, so face that way and look back over the town.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x (or panorama mode) to grab the whole scene, then try 1x for a balanced frame. Zoom 2x or 5x to pick the hotel out of the rooftops; how far you can go depends on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the hotel, then drag the slider down a touch to make the picture a bit darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Reviewers say the view is especially good around sunset, when the city lights come on. Get there a little early to practise your frames while the light is still soft, then switch on night mode once it's dark.
card.selfie_here: Head to the colonial front of Queen's Hotel on the D S Senanayake Veediya street side, which a guided night photo tour uses as its main posing backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the hotel over your shoulder. The exact spot is approximate, so wander a little to find your angle.
card.rules_and_safety: The hotel is a working business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or photograph from its grounds. Kandy View Point appears to be free to enter, but check on the day.
card.challenge: Can you fit the lake, the temple area and the hotel all into one frame, with your horizon dead level?
card.good_to_know: The building began as a royal residence, the Dullawe Walauwa, built for King Sri Wickrama Rajasinha. After the British defeated the Kandyan Kingdom in 1815 it became a mansion for the Governor of Ceylon, and it took the name Queens Hotel in 1869. Today it's a 90-room British Colonial style hotel with more than 160 years of history.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the terrace at Kandy View Point, on higher ground south-east of the centre. The hotel lies to the north-west, about 1.7 km away in a straight line, so face that way and look back over the town.

selfie_spots.name: Colonial facade of Queen's Hotel, on D S Senanayake Veediya
selfie_spots.detail: in front of the hotel's colonial front, on the D S Senanayake Veediya street side
selfie_spots.why: A guided night photo tour uses this facade as its main posing backdrop, so it is an established photo stop.

The GetYourGuide page names the hotel facade as a posing backdrop but gives no exact stand-point, so the position is approximate. No page I found names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole hotel in frame, so ask_someone_spot is null. Sources give two street addresses for the hotel (D S Senanayake Veediya and No 4 Dalada Veediya), which are the same frontage on different listings. Other pages (Tripadvisor photo captions, hotel listings) mention the lake, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic opposite, and the hotel's terrace and garden, but none describe a selfie or photo spot there. No page I found gives selfie stick or tripod rules, or a safety point for this location.

card.hook: It's a plain, tall, four-storey factory with no fancy bits, and that's exactly why it looks so good on your phone. Wait until you step inside and find the old machines.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Ceylon Tea Museum in Hanthana, about 3 km south of the centre of Kandy, where the phone icon is. Walk back across the open ground outside until the whole factory fits, then face the building.
card.zoom: Outside, tap zoom 0.5x to fit all four floors in one shot. Indoors, switch to 1x for machines and rooms, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for dials, rollers and labels.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the walls so the building stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the museum is open and quieter, so you can take your time indoors. For the outside shot, soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the top-floor tea café and take your selfie on the terrace with the green hills behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little higher, and let the view fill the background. Down below, the landscaped gardens with their different tea plants make a colourful backdrop too.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for what's open and whether photography is allowed in every area. If Google suggests a walking route along an overgrown forest trail from the Hulan Ground path, it may be a bit dangerous, so use the road instead.
card.challenge: Find a row of old machines and fit three repeating shapes into one frame, like wheels, belts or dryer doors. Bonus points if it looks like a pattern.
card.good_to_know: The Hanthana Tea Factory was built in 1925. The area was one of the first to grow tea successfully after coffee failed in Sri Lanka. The factory stood abandoned for more than a decade before it reopened as a museum on 1 December 2001, and inside you'll find exhibits on tea pioneers like James Taylor and Thomas Lipton.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Ceylon Tea Museum in Hanthana, about 3 km south of the centre of Kandy, where the phone icon is. Walk back across the open ground outside until the whole factory fits, then face the building.

card.hook: Picture a hillside house so packed with antiques, murals and family photos that the hotel calls itself an 'anti-hotel'. That wonderfully crowded character is why the front of Helga's Folly is the photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, at the front of Helga's Folly where the drive climbs up from Rajaphilla Mawatha. Face the building, so the drive leads your eye up to it and the jungle and lake-side setting sit behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If the drive and the building won't fit in one frame, go to 0.5x. Try zoom 2x to 5x for details like the murals and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, use the drive as a line pointing at the front door, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early evening is lovely here. The light is soft and kind to the colours of the building.
card.selfie_here: Try the front entrance of Helga's Folly, which visitors often photograph. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and tuck the building in behind your shoulder. Check the result on the spot and adjust.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a private hotel and restaurant, so ask at reception before you start photographing. Keep your shots to the front, because the rear is reported to have been damaged in a recent cyclone. One visitor also warns that monkeys can get into rooms within minutes, so keep balcony doors locked if you're staying.
card.challenge: Can you fit the drive, the whole front of the building and a slice of jungle behind it in one frame, with the walls perfectly straight?
card.good_to_know: Helga's Folly is an Art Nouveau boutique hotel, designed by Esme de Silva in the 1930s as the family home. In the mid-1990s her daughter, Helga de Silva Blow Perera, inherited it and gave it the name it has today. Inside, it's filled with antiques, murals and family photographs.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, at the front of Helga's Folly where the drive climbs up from Rajaphilla Mawatha. Face the building, so the drive leads your eye up to it and the jungle and lake-side setting sit behind.

selfie_spots.why: Visitor photo sets label the entrance as a shot, and a hotel gallery includes a front-of-property view that a guide says suits evening photography.

card.hook: Two eras are squeezed into one station here. Out front, a curvy Art Moderne building with a clock tower. Behind it, a much older Victorian platform roof full of arches and fine metalwork.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Kandy railway station building, then step back to the forecourt or the road in front. Face the station so the whole front, with its clock tower and arched windows, fits in the shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full front of the building. Switch to zoom 0.5x when you're inside to fit in the arched platform roof, and use zoom 2x to pick out the clock and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines so the walls and clock tower stay straight, and if the sky looks washed out, tap the building and slide it a touch darker.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, when there are fewer people in the frame. It's also the easiest time to get a clean look along the platform.
card.selfie_here: Hold your phone with the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x, and tilt it up a little so the clock tower and arched front sit over your shoulder. Do it from the forecourt, well away from the tracks.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working station on a live train line, with electricity pylons along the side. Stay behind the platform safety line, and never lean out when a train is moving. Check with Sri Lanka Railways before any professional or commercial shoot.
card.challenge: Catch a train arriving or leaving with the platform arches behind it, and try a Live Photo so you can pick your best frame afterwards.
card.good_to_know: The first steam engine reached Kandy on 16 April 1867, and the first passenger service began on 1 August 1867. The station sits about 512 m above sea level and 120 km from Colombo, which is why trains here feel like part of the hill-country journey.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Kandy railway station building, then step back to the forecourt or the road in front. Face the station so the whole front, with its clock tower and arched windows, fits in the shot.

selfie_research.safety: Pages warn that the station is on a live train line with electricity pylons along the side, and that leaning out when a train is moving fast is risky (Aga on the run).
selfie_research.notes: I found no page that names a spot where a visitor can take a selfie with Kandy railway station behind them, so I left selfie_spots empty rather than guess. Airial's guide mentions the platforms and the colonial architecture as photo backdrops, but it names no specific spot. The closest named selfie location is Kandy View Point (Arthur's Seat) on Rajapihilla Mawatha, reached by tuk-tuk or a steep walk. Its pages describe views of Kandy Lake and the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, and none mention the railway station in the frame, so I did not list it as a selfie spot for this landmark. Distances from the city centre vary by source (about 1.1 km to 1.7 km). No page I found gives rules on selfie sticks or tripods, and no page describes a spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole station in view, so ask_someone_spot is null. Sources: Airial, Kandy Railway Station (https://www.airial.travel/attractions/sri-lanka/kandy/kandy-railway-station-Lh9LWHaT); Aga on the run, How to take the perfect train photo in Sri Lanka (https://agaonthe.run/how-to-take-train-photo-in-sri-lanka/); Avian Experiences, Kandy View Point (https://avianexperiences.com/attractions/kandy-view-point); Airial, Kandy View Point Arthur's Seat (https://airial.travel/attractions/sri-lanka/kandy/kandy-view-point-arthurs-seat-3Io6Al0V); Sri Lanka Explorers, Kandy View Point (https://srilankaexplorers.com/a-tourists-guide-to-kandy-view-point/).

card.hook: Here's the honest bit: from up here the Royal Palace is a small guest at a very big party. The real star is the whole scene, with Kandy Lake, the Temple of the Tooth and green hills all in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kandy View Point, the viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha above the city. Face north-west, where the old royal palace area sits close to the temple and the edge of Kandy Lake.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full sweep of lake, temple and hills. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the palace roofs and the temple beside them. Use 0.5x only when you want lots of sky and hillside.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the lake on the lower third. Then tap the lake or the temple and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or sunset, when the light is soft and the city lights start to come on. At dusk, try night mode and rest your arms on the railing to keep your phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head down to the palace courtyard and stand in front of the carved palace walls, facing the Temple of the Tooth. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more carving, and hold the phone a bit higher than usual.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Kandy Lake shore beside the Royal Palace and ask a passer-by to step back and frame you with the whole complex, ideally near sunset.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the palace complex, but some areas have limits, so check the signs at each entrance. Don't pose with your back to a shrine or Buddha image, and don't photograph inside the temple's inner sanctum. Cover your shoulders and knees.
card.challenge: Catch the lake on the lower third with a tree branch or a bit of railing in the corner, so your photo looks like it has real depth.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Palace was the official home of the Kandyan kings until British rule began in 1815. It has been destroyed and rebuilt several times, including in 1634 under Rajasinha II. Only a handful of buildings survive, including the Royal Audience Hall (construction began in 1783) and the King's Palace, now a museum. The complex is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Kandy View Point, the viewing platform on Rajapihilla Mawatha above the city. Face north-west, where the old royal palace area sits close to the temple and the edge of Kandy Lake.

selfie_research.notes: No page found gives a selfie spot with the Royal Palace clearly behind the subject, so both selfie spots are the best named options and their backdrops are unconfirmed. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, so none are reported. Sources conflict on Royal Palace Park: one describes a hilltop park with lake views, while another calls it a garden of the temple complex, so it was not used. card.hook: Kandy's old kings kept this forest to themselves, and the leaves still seem to guard the view. You won't get one big open panorama up here. You get peeks of the city and lake through gaps in the trees, like the forest is teasing you.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the summit of the reserve's highest peak, Flag Point (also called Kodimale), which you reach by the Kodimale trail. Face out through the trees towards Kandy city and the lake below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the city and lake peeking through the trees. Try 0.5x for the forest canopy and the trail, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the lake or some rooftops through a gap in the leaves.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the distant city (not the leaves in front of you), then slide the brightness a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the view.
card.best_time: Guides recommend morning, about 7 to 10 AM, or late afternoon. Both are comfortable times for the climb.
card.selfie_here: Stop at the break in the foliage where the forest path climbs up to the City Viewpoint. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the town and lake are over your shoulder, with the forest closing in around you.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the marked paths and respect the boundaries of any active meditation hermitages. Paths can be slippery after rain and leeches can turn up in wet weather, so wear shoes with good grip. There's an entry fee, at least for foreign visitors, and trail conditions can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a gap in the leaves where the lake shows through, and make the leaves a proper frame around it. Bonus points if you didn't have to hold a branch out of the way.
card.good_to_know: Udawattakele is a 104-hectare forest on a hill ridge right in the city. In the days of the Kandyan kings it was the garden above the royal palace, which is why it was once called the Forbidden Forest. It became a forest reserve in 1856 and a sanctuary in 1938, and today it's known for its birds and giant lianas. The summit ridge is 635 metres above sea level, about 115 metres above Kandy Lake.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the summit of the reserve's highest peak, Flag Point (also called Kodimale), which you reach by the Kodimale trail. Face out through the trees towards Kandy city and the lake below.

selfie_spots.name: City Viewpoint on the uphill forest path, Udawattakele
selfie_spots.detail: at the break in the foliage where the forest path climbs up to the City Viewpoint
selfie_spots.why: Reaching it means climbing through the forest, so a visitor standing at the opening can have the reserve behind them with the town and lake in front.

sources.title: What to do in Kandy - Our Guide to Sri Lanka's Ancient Capital — Adventures of Jellie

selfie_research.safety: Visitors should remain on marked paths and respect the boundaries of active meditation hermitages.
selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was found. The Adventures of Jellie page places the City Viewpoint at the forest's break in foliage and says its selfie was taken at 'Kandy's viewpoint', which may refer to the lake-side Kandy Viewpoint rather than this one, so the forest-behind framing is my inference, not stated. Kandy View Point (Arthur's Seat, Rajapihilla Mawatha) was found, but its pages describe the city as the backdrop, and one says the reserve is visible on one side only, so I did not list it as a selfie spot. No page names a spot where a passer-by can frame the whole reserve, so ask_someone_spot is null. No page gives a selfie stick rule for this site. One review advises 'take a strong tripod' for photography, which is advice rather than a rule, so it is omitted. The Tripadvisor page mentions 'Take a strong tripod' and an early-morning lake visit, but gives no rule.

card.hook: The Kandy Clock Tower sits right in the middle of a busy junction, with traffic and people flowing around its base like a stream round a rock. That flow is half the fun, so don't zoom in on the clock face too soon.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Sri Dalada Veediya and S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha, at the street junction by the tower's base. Face the tower so the whole thing fits in, with the crossing traffic and people around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower and the busy junction. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view of the tower alone, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the clock face and the carved details higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and hold your phone upright and level so the tower's sides stay straight, then tap the tower and slide a little darker if the sky looks too bright.
card.best_time: Late afternoon towards sunset is lovely, when the tower can stand against the hills with street life below. Give yourself a minute to check the frame first, because the scene changes constantly.
card.selfie_here: A local guide says the north side of the tower gives the best photos, so try it: stand on that side with the tower behind you and the hills in front. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a little low and out so the tower rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to frame the whole tower from the pavement in front of the Bank of Ceylon Kandy branch, while you stand with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The junction is very busy with traffic and pedestrians, so stay on the pavement, let people pass, and take care when stepping towards the road to frame a shot. There's nowhere to sit nearby, so plan to take your photos quickly.
card.challenge: Get the whole tower in the frame with one person crossing the street at its base, and call it your 'Kandy in one shot' photo.
card.good_to_know: Haji Mohamed Ismail built the tower in 1950 as a monument to his son, Mohamed Zacky Ismail, who died in a landslide accident at Kadugannawa in 1947. The clock machinery came from the United Kingdom, and the tower was finished on 23 December 1950, though it wasn't officially opened until the following year. Architect Shirley de Alwis used the Kandyan style and worked in elements of the Temple of the Tooth and the king's palace.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Sri Dalada Veediya and S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike Mawatha, at the street junction by the tower's base. Face the tower so the whole thing fits in, with the crossing traffic and people around it.

selfie_spots.why: A local guide quoted on one page says the north side gives the best photos, with the sun setting over the hills behind the city.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot for a selfie with the tower behind the person. The selfie spot is the north side the local guide recommends for photos, which is an inference and not a confirmed selfie position. The Kandy Lake and surrounding-hills backdrops mentioned by one guide describe what the camera sees, not a named standing spot, so I left them out. The Bank of Ceylon page only gives the tower's location, not where a photo was taken, so the passer-by spot is also doubtful. No page gives selfie-stick or tripod rules. card.hook: Here's a Kandy surprise: the best view of Malwathu Maha Viharaya isn't from inside the grounds, it's from across the water. Stand by the lake and you get calm water, a strip of shoreline, then rooftops and trees stacked up behind.
card.stand_here: Stand on Sangaraja Mawatha, where the road meets the Kandy Lake promenade. The monastery is just south of it, about 1 minute on foot, so face the monastery with the lake in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the monastery, the shore and the lake in one shot. Go to 0.5x for more water and sky, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the rooftops and trees across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the shoreline on the lower line so the lake fills the bottom, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light suits lake views best. Midday sun can make the water glare, so tap the monastery buildings and slide the brightness down a touch if you're there then.
card.selfie_here: Try the lake-side walkway on the Kandy Lake promenade beside the Malwatta monastery, at the Sangaraja Mawatha end. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your phone a bit low and angle it so the lake and the monastery rooftops sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a living monastery, so photograph the buildings from outside and ask before taking pictures of any monks. Ask locally before you go inside, because it's an active place of worship.
card.challenge: Take your monastery shot, then turn around and see if you can spot the Temple of the Tooth and the Udawattekele forest from the same stretch.
card.good_to_know: Malwathu Maha Viharaya is a working Buddhist monastery and the headquarters of the Malwatta Chapter of the Siyam Nikaya. It shares custodianship of the sacred tooth relic at the Sri Dalada Maligawa with one other monastery. It's believed to have been founded by Senasammatha Vikramabahu in the late 15th or early 16th century, and its oldest part, the Poyamalu Viharaya, is an archaeologically protected monument.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Sangaraja Mawatha, where the road meets the Kandy Lake promenade. The monastery is just south of it, about 1 minute on foot, so face the monastery with the lake in front of you.

selfie_spots.name: Kandy Lake promenade beside Malwatta monastery (Sangaraja Mawatha end)
selfie_spots.detail: on the lake-side walkway near the Malwatta monastery, at the end of Sangaraja Mawatha where the lake promenade meets the monastery
selfie_spots.why: Pages describe the lake bank near the monastery as a photo subject and say the vihara overlooks the lake from this stretch, but none explicitly names it as a selfie spot with the vihara behind the visitor.

sources.title: Sri Lanka View: Kandy Town, Kandyan History, Architecture, Tourist attractions
A stroll around Kandy Lake (Sunday Observer)

selfie_research.notes: Low confidence overall. No page I found names a spot where the visitor stands with the whole Malwathu Maha Viharaya behind them, and no page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph the whole landmark, so ask_someone_spot is null. The selfie spot above is inferred from lake-bank photo captions and a walk description, not from a stated selfie recommendation. Kandy Viewpoint (Arthur's Seat, Rajapihilla Mawatha) is well documented but its pages show the Temple of the Tooth and lake, not Malwathu, so I excluded it. One page says parts of the complex remain working religious spaces rather than general visitor areas, so visitors should check before entering the grounds. No page I found gives selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Picture a bright white pagoda with green hills rolling out behind it and village rooftops peeking through, all above Kandy Lake. This is the view that makes the uphill walk worth it.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, which marks the spot at Asgiri Maha Viharaya on the north side of Kandy Lake. Face the white pagoda so the hills and rooftops fill the space behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pagoda and the hills into one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the pagoda, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops and ridgelines.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pagoda, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white stays crisp and detailed instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white pagoda. Try to skip the harsh middle of the day, when all that white can glare on your screen.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steep steps up from the road to the outer circular balcony around the stupa. Use the front camera, keep the stupa behind you and the city in view, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more in.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working monastery, so dress modestly and be ready to take your shoes off in sacred areas. Photos are fine outdoors and around the stupa, but not inside the shrine halls or during worship. Ask first before photographing monks, and check opening hours before you go.
card.challenge: Walk the path around the pagoda and find the one clear gap where the white stupa stands out against the green hills.
card.good_to_know: King Parakramabahu IV (reigned 1305 to 1335) had this monastery founded by Commander Siriwardhana. It's made up of several temples, including the Meda Pansala (1767) and the Aluth Viharaya, built a year later. The grounds also hold a 36-foot recumbent Buddha carved from rock and the old royal cremation ground of the Kandyan kings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, which marks the spot at Asgiri Maha Viharaya on the north side of Kandy Lake. Face the white pagoda so the hills and rooftops fill the space behind it.

selfie_spots.name: Outer circular balcony around the stupa, Asgiri Maha Viharaya
selfie_spots.detail: on the balcony that wraps around the outside of the stupa, reached after climbing the steep steps up from the road; keep the stupa behind you and the city in view
selfie_spots.why: A travel blog describes a circular balcony around the stupa that gives views over the city, so the white stupa can sit behind a selfie with the valley below.

sources.title: What to do in Kandy - Our Guide to Sri Lanka's Ancient Capital — Adventures of Jellie
Asgiriya Maha Viharaya Kandy (2025)

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by the pages I found; the 'walk around the pagoda' views from the Airial guide describe the same outdoor circuit, so I did not list it separately. No page I found names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole complex, so ask_someone_spot is null. A Tripadvisor snippet calling a photo 'perfect for views' with the painted temple roof refers to Bahirawakanda, a different temple, so I excluded it. A 3Pulse listing shows a 'Temple viewpoint' about 409 m away, but no page says it frames this temple, so I left it out. The Asgiri Maha Viharaya is a living monastery: one guide advises asking before photographing monks, interiors or ceremonies, and another advises avoiding photos of ceremonies without permission. No page I found mentions selfie sticks or tripods.

card.hook: The crowds around the Temple of the Tooth can be a lot, so walk a little west and let a calm wall of red brick settle your shoulders. St. Paul's Neo-Gothic front is warm, quiet and very kind to a phone camera.
card.stand_here: Stand on Deva Veediya, directly in front of the church entrance on the road side, and face east. The red-brick front fills your view, but keep clear of the doorway.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole front in. If the pavement keeps you too close, tap 0.5x and stay square on to the building so the edges don't stretch. Save 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the brickwork and windows.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines so the walls stand straight, and if the sky is bright, tap the brick wall and slide a bit darker so the red keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the brick and fewer people on the street. Avoid service times, like Saturday prayers, because the entrance needs to stay clear.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low and out in front of you so the building fits over your shoulder. Step back from the doorway first so nobody has to squeeze past you.
card.rules_and_safety: Taking photos of the outside is fine, but photography inside the church isn't allowed. It's a working church, so don't block the entrance, and ask first if staff or worshippers are nearby. If you want the churchyard, check on arrival that it's open to visitors.
card.challenge: Walk to the side of the church and fit three window bays in a row into one straight, gridline-perfect shot.
card.good_to_know: St. Paul's is an Anglican church, built mainly from solid terracotta bricks. The foundation stone was laid on 16 March 1843 and it was consecrated on 25 January 1853. British officials and the garrison used it first, which is why it's also called the Garrison Church. Inside is the only pipe organ in Kandy, a replacement from a closed church in Bradford that arrived in 2009.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Deva Veediya, directly in front of the church entrance on the road side, and face east. The red-brick front fills your view, but keep clear of the doorway.

rules.rule: Photography is generally not allowed inside the church; visitors are asked not to take pictures in the sacred space.

sources.title: St. Paul's Church Kandy (2026), Airial

rules.rule: Taking photos of the church's exterior is permitted, according to this guide.

sources.title: St. Paul's Church Kandy (2026), Airial

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific spot where a visitor can stand with St. Paul's Church behind them, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole church in frame, so both fields are left empty rather than guessed. The Airial guide says the exterior offers good views but names no location. A Tripadvisor review mentions a coffee bar just in front of the church, west of the Temple of the Tooth, but no page gives it as a photo spot, so I did not use it. No page states any selfie-stick or tripod rule, and no safety point was mentioned. Sources disagree on the church's denomination: Tripadvisor reviews call it Catholic in some places, while Wikidata and other pages call it Anglican. The address given is 10 Deva Veediya, Kandy, which matches the coordinates provided.

card.hook: Picture a small, layered tile roof sitting calmly on a stone terrace, with the Royal Palace complex behind it. Natha Devale looks quiet, but it's thought to be the oldest surviving building in Kandy.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the front of Natha Devale, on the raised stone terrace facing the Temple of the Tooth, and face the front of the shrine. Keep the open terrace and the palace complex behind it in the picture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for one wide shot that shows the shrine in its setting. Then go to 2x (or 5x if your phone has it) for the roofline and doorway. Don't push past your phone's zoom buttons, because the picture goes soft.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the shrine on one vertical line with the terrace in the lower third, and keep the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more even light. If you want to catch the Esala Perahera, check the dates first and expect big crowds.
card.selfie_here: Head to the carved stone gateway at the compound entrance (the Vahalkada, with its dragon arch). Use the front camera and stand in front of it so the gateway is behind you. Try 0.5x if your phone offers it, to fit more of the carving in.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a place of worship, so dress modestly and be quiet and respectful. Photography is generally allowed, but ask before taking close-ups of devotees or monks. Don't use flash inside the inner shrine, and check signs or ask a temple official, because photos inside are often restricted.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the same shrine: one wide with the palace terrace, one close-up of the roof and doorway. Then see which one your friends like more.
card.good_to_know: Tradition says Natha Devale was here before the Tooth Relic arrived in Kandy. It's believed to have been built by King Vikramabahu III in the 14th century. Natha means 'lord' or 'protector', and in the days of the Kandyan kings, royal names were given here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the front of Natha Devale, on the raised stone terrace facing the Temple of the Tooth, and face the front of the shrine. Keep the open terrace and the palace complex behind it in the picture.

selfie_spots.why: A travel guide names the intricately carved stone gateway as a prime photo opportunity, and the entrance is a roofed structure with guard stones and a dragon arch.
